title: Elucidation of Human Genetic Landscape Considering Glacial Periods and Polymorphic Loci–DNA Linkage: An Out-of-Africa Hypothesis-Free Model
content: Humans have sparse, fine body hair and are more vulnerable to cold than heat. During glacial periods, individuals carrying cold‑resistance polymorphic loci in their DNA were more likely to survive. The frequency of these loci, together with other loci linked to them on the same DNA copy, gradually rose in the population. By contrast, alternative DNA copies without cold‑resistance loci and the polymorphisms they harbored were progressively lost. This ultimately reduced genetic diversity and intensified genomic homogenization. Eurasia, the Americas and Oceania were impacted by cold surges during glacial periods, so populations there share some cold‑tolerance polymorphic loci. More severe cold brought stronger selective pressure, greater enrichment of cold‑adaptive loci, deeper vertical branches on DNA phylogenetic trees, and lower genetic diversity. Most of Africa lies near the Equator at relatively high elevations and experienced limited glacial impact. Consequently, human genetic diversity there is higher, and not all individuals carry cold‑tolerance polymorphic loci. This paper explains the human genetic landscape without relying on the Out‑of‑Africa hypothesis. It also points out that the methods used to define Neanderthal‑specific sequences contain flaws, so the corresponding findings cannot serve as evidence for admixture between modern humans and Neanderthals. Lastly, it argues that the abundance of hominin fossils in Africa does not support the claim that Africa is the homeland of human origins.
